Question: Are the Na’vis classified as mammals?
Answer: No. Mammalia is a Class/Clade in Terrestrial taxonomy. A clade, by definition, consists of an organism and all of its descendants. The Na’vi do not descend from the first mammal, therefore they are not mammals. No extraterrestrial falls into any of the classifications we use for Earth life. There are no extraterrestrial animals, plants, or fungi. They did not descend from our LUCA. They don’t fall into Domain Archaea, Bacteria, or Eukaryota. They descend from a different last universal common ancestor entirely, and their taxonomic tree would therefore be completely different. Even if they were to look exactly like us (so tremendously unlikely), they would be less closely related to us than we are to the most bizarre and different bacterium that has ever existed. They’re less closely related to us than we are to any of our viruses.

Question: Is it possible for animals to create hybrids with other species, regardless of whether they have a common ancestor?
Answer: Every single thing on Earth has a common ancestor. We all descend from LUCA (the Last Universal Common Ancestor). It’s only a question of how far back in time that ancestor lived. Species that can hybridize within the same Genus are common. Species that can hybridize with members of another genus are less common, but there are definitely a good number of them. Species that can hybridize with a member of a higher clade (above the level of Genus) are pretty rare. The less closely related species are, the more likely it is that their genes won’t line up correctly to create a viable organism. (Helmeted Guinea Fowl (Numididae Numida meleagris) crossed with Domestic Chicken (Phasianidae Gallus gallus domesticus. These birds are in different Linnaean Families/clades above the level of Genus. As you can see, the hybrid offspring are healthy, and look like what they are - half chicken, half guinea fowl).

Question: Why do evolutionists prefer to pick on the bonobos for comparison with humans, instead of the more intelligent chimpanzees?
Answer: First, there is no such thing as an ‘evolutionist.’ That’s a term that implies that acceptance of settled science is some sort of belief system or that there is some question about evolutionary theory. That is not the case. There are people who accept science, and science-deniers. Science denial is irrational. There is no need for special names for people who accept settled science based on which science they accept. Presumably, if they accept settled science on evolution, they accept settled science on everything else, too. lol. I think part of the issue stems from the fact that in common language, a theory is a speculation - a guess. But scientific terms have different definitions, and the term ‘theory’ in science means ‘an explanation for observed facts which is thoroughly supported by ample evidence, and has no contradictory evidence against it.’ First, a hypothesis is proposed - an explanation for facts we have observed. Then the hypothesis is rigorously tested, and evidence is collected. If the evidence all supports the hypothesis, and none disproves it, then it becomes a theory. Once the body of evidence becomes truly overwhelming and massive, then we say that it is a Proven Theory. Evolutionary theory is a proven theory - it is the closest that science can ever come to producing an absolute truth. There are no remaining doubts about it. Not even one. There is no evidence that does not support it. None at all. So, if you want to question accepted science, then you need to actual do science and research. You need to present material facts that contradict the hypothesis or theory, and they need to have been collected using rational, rigorous methods. You need to actually scientifically DISPROVE a theory in order to effectively overturn it. Anything else is meaningless nonsense; irrational behavior based in pretending that reality is not what it is. And no, believing someone else who said they did the work is not sufficient. You have to actually explore and understand their work, and it has to have been duplicated and verified. No one takes anyone at their word. Belief should never have a role to play in any of this. Science is about using a rational method to explore reality and find out what it really is. It does not include faith/absolute certainty, ever. I wanted to make this clear before moving on to the next part of your question, because you went on to state a couple more things that weren’t true. First you said that scientists (this is what you really meant) choose to compare humans and bonobos rather than humans and chimps. This is simply not true. Both species are compared to humans, and their cognition is studied to aid our understanding of our own evolution. Next, you said that chimpanzees are more intelligent than bonobos. This is also not true. Intelligence is not all one thing, and these two species have different intellectual strengths and weaknesses from each other, as well as from us. Bonobos are far more skilled at solving tasks that relate to the theory of mind and social causality, while chimps are more skilled at solving tasks that relate to tool use and physical causality. In short, bonobos are better at knowing themselves and others, while chimps are better at understanding physics. Chimpanzees are far more aggressive than bonobos, and this holds them back to some degree. They are, in fact, more aggressive than humans, having a significantly higher rate of reactive aggression. Bonobos, conversely, are about equal to humans in reactive aggression. Chimps also have a higher rate of proactive aggression than humans do, but humans have a higher rate of proactive aggression than Bonobos. To put this into perspective, a chimp is smart enough to sharpen a stick to stab you with because you made him angry by grinning at him. And he’ll do it, too. lol. A bonobo is smart enough to understand that you aren’t a bonobo and your body language is different from his, so he doesn’t have any reason to be angry that you grinned at him. Which one is ‘smarter?’ I will also leave you with the fact that humans are not superior in all areas of cognition to our closest relatives. As I pointed out, cognition is not all one thing. And we don’t win in every area. Chimpanzees wipe the floor with us in tests of working memory. No contest. Even when we have time to practice, they still beat us. They are simply BETTER at noting where things are, exactly, and remembering it five minutes later when they can’t see those things anymore. As for bonobos - a bonobo was able to recognize both her sister and her nephew in photographs after not having seen either one for 26 years, which is the longest term social memory documented in a non-human animal. (I don’t think the working memory of bonobos has been tested, yet). So, we have very good reasons to study the cognitive abilities of both species, as an aid to understanding how various parts of the brain work, and how our own cognitive arrangement likely evolved.

Question: Why do people self-diagnose themselves with autism? I’m autistic, and my entire life has revolved around hiding it. People do treat me differently based on whether they know. Whether or not you have it: why would you want to draw attention to it?
Answer: Because most of us who have self-diagnosed autism are old. Too old for the currently available tests to be valid - that’s literally what psychologists say, by the way. They go on a lot about how all of the tests were DESIGNED for children, and don’t work so well for adults. That’s why self-diagnosis is so accepted - because psychologists have essentially given it a tentative thumbs-up as being as valid as anything. By our age, we have learned a whole lot of masking, and that can make professional diagnosis a lot more challenging. Because most of us were able to cope in school, at least in some limping fashion, we weren’t diagnosed. We were generally able to care for ourselves and hold down jobs. But there were always some things we struggled with, and we never understood why. Discovering that we are autistic is generally a huge relief. We finally understand WHY we struggled with those things. It’s not because we didn’t try hard enough, and it’s not a personality flaw. We aren’t lazy, or necessarily antisocial - autism is the reason. And once we know that, we can develop ways of coping with those issues that often never occurred to us before. So the label has sincerely helped us to help ourselves, even though we don’t usually need professional help from others. As for drawing attention to it - we’re too old to care what others think of us. Besides, if by vigorously advocating we can get allistic people to change their minds about how they regard autistic people in general, we can help younger autistic people who may have more trouble masking by creating a better cultural environment for them. I’ve seen a lot of pointless misunderstandings that would have been avoided if one of the people had simply said ‘I’m autistic, so I’m not sure whether I’m missing something,’ or ‘I’m autistic, so I really can’t tolerate that kind of touch/sound/scent/etc.’

Question: What are some animals that resemble dinosaurs in some way other than size and appearance (like behavior etc.)? Why do they resemble them so closely?
Answer: Crocodilians resemble some dinosaurs in behavior. For example, some crocodilians incubate their eggs by building a mound of decaying vegetation, and laying their eggs inside. They can add more or reduce layers to adjust the temperatures inside, and guard their eggs from predators. This is exactly how a modern dinosaur, the brush turkey, incubates its eggs as well. And crocodilians look after their young after they hatch, providing protection when their young call for them. Some birds, such as chickens, do the same. (Birds are dinosaurs). Additionally, crocodilians, like dinosaurs, have one-way respiratory systems, and four-chambered hearts. The reason why they resemble dinosaurs so closely in physiology and behavior is because they are both Archosaurs, and are very closely related compared with other animals. (In terms of appearance, crocodiles and dinosaurs don’t look very much alike).

Question: How do mRNA vaccines simulate an infection and train the immune system for when it encounters the real virus?
Answer: The vaccine introduced mRNA to the body. Messenger RNA enters a cell, and directs the cell’s machinery to produce a specific protein This protein is the same as that found in the virus. The cell produces and releases the protein into the bloodstream. The immune system notices a weird protein, immediately goes on the attack, creating antibodies to combat it. After a few days, the messenger RNA in the cell is discarded and it receives new messenger RNA instructions via your body’s own systems. It returns to its normal activities. (Messenger RNA has a short lifespan, as your body is always adjusting what it tells your cells to do). If the actual virus shows up, your immune system is already locked and loaded to attack and destroy it.

Question: How can I heat up my snake tank? I have a ball python and the power just went out and its 34 degrees outside. I fed him this morning and would rather not move his whole enclosure. Do I have any options to keep him warm?
Answer: This is an emergency situation. Your ball python should not be exposed to temperatures under 70F at all, and temperatures under 60F are EXTREMELY dangerous. Remove the ball python from its enclosure, and tie it in a pillow case. You can warm up your car and keep the snake warm there until you have the supplies you need. If you have an insulated box used for shipping reptiles, put the snake in it with a hand warmer. Wrap the hand warmer carefully in a thick towel so the snake cannot be burned. (Hand warmers typically get too hot for any sort of direct contact). You can also use a cooler, just open the water vent hole to let fresh air in, or punch a small hole in the side with a pencil if it is styrofoam. (You don’t need more than one hole - snakes require much less oxygen than a bird or mammal, and more holes would compromise the insulation). Use an indoor/outdoor thermometer with a probe to keep track of the temperature inside of the cooler or box. It’s important that it never falls below 70F or above 90F. For the future, buy an insulated reptile shipping box the right size for your snake. Keep it, a pillowcase or snake bag, and a supply of two or three 40 hour reptile shipping heat packs (you can buy them online). The 24 hour kind aren’t as safe (they spike hotter), so get the 40 hour at minimum. That way, if the power goes out, you will have the right supplies on hand to keep your snake safe. A snake can be kept in a shipping box for up to two days if necessary. After that, you will need to give the opportunity to drink water. If your snake has been exposed to temperatures under 70F, observe it VERY carefully for the next week for symptoms of respiratory infection. If you see the snake sitting with its head angled up or mouth open, see bubbly spit in its mouth, or hear it rasp (or feel a rattle when holding it when it breathes) take it to a reptile vet immediately. (Respiratory infections can generally be easily treated with a course of antibiotics if caught early, but are likely to prove deadly if not treated).

Question: If it is true that humans came from previously existing, lower lifeforms, why has this evolution not continued?
Answer: Evolution never actually stops - the term refers to a continuous process. Sometimes evolution occurs faster, and sometimes more slowly, but it’s always happening. The term ‘evolution’ in reference to organisms means ‘changes that occur in a population over time.’ This distinguishes it from changes that occur in individuals. A population is a contiguous breeding group of organisms of the same species. Evolution begins when mutations occur, hybridization occurs, or horizontal gene transfer occurs in a single organism in the group. If that change is detrimental, that may mean that the organism doesn’t survive to breed, or breeds less successfully than organisms without that change. So, either immediately or after a few generations, all individuals with that change will be eliminated. This is called ‘purifying’ or ‘negative’ selection. It’s an important part of the evolutionary process, and helps a species maintain its integrity over time. If the change that occurs in the individual is neutral or beneficial, then the organism has a better chance of survival (though bad luck can still strike). It may have more offspring than the others that don’t have the beneficial mutation. (Or the same amount, if the change is neutral). Sometimes a neutral change will proliferate through the population if the one that carries it has other genes that improve its survival potential. A beneficial change will often proliferate much faster, as the individual’s offspring will, in turn, have more breeding success, and so on. So the organism that don’t have the mutation will mate with the ones that do, and their carrier offspring will survive better than the non-carriers, until finally the entire population has the beneficial change. But there isn’t just one of these changes happening at a time - there are typically many of them, being positively and negatively reinforced in the population all at once. This is responsible for the diversity in individuals that you see. Not all deer in an area look the same - some are bigger, some smaller, some more gracile, some sturdier, their coats may be different colors, etc etc. That is the result of the evolutionary process at work. For a species to evolve into an entire new species takes a very long time in most cases. Except when it doesn’t - every once in a while, hybridization (an important part of evolution’s tool chest) can produce a new species practically overnight! And we’ve been privileged to be paying attention in just the right place, at the right time, to see it happen before our very eyes. This new species is fragile, but is expanding its population and appears sturdy. An example of hybrid speciation - evolution in action, right in front of us! Another potential new species is in the process of evolving in the Eastern United States. Presently considered to be ‘coyotes,’ the Eastern Coyote is a species with variable amounts of wolf and dog genes from hybrid matings. (Typically the animals are no less than 60% coyote - usually closer to 80%). From wolves, they gain greater size and better cooperative/pack hunting behaviors. From domestic dogs they gain the ability to understand human behavior and a tolerance for human-modified areas. This makes them ideal predators to take the place of extirpated gray wolves. They can live in our parks and golf courses, and eat the bountiful numbers of rodents, squirrels, and rabbits that proliferate there due to low numbers of other predators. They’re also large enough to take white tail deer fawns. As evolution continues to select them, they will no doubt become better deer hunters, and also be less prone to behavior that puts them in conflict with humans (as those individuals that behave that way are often eliminated from the gene pool). The Western coyote, ancestor of these animals, is smaller, and a solitary hunter that lives only with its mate. Pups stay with their parents only until fully grown, the disperse. The Eastern Coyote is often seen in packs. As for human evolution, there are many examples of our continued changing within populations. Homo sapiens, our species, is only around 300,000 years old. Question: Is there a reason why dinosaurs did not evolve into mammals instead of reptiles?
Answer: Nothing evolves into the same thing twice. Evolution is a complex process involving random mutations and selective pressures. The first amniotes, animals that had a membrane inside their eggs to keep them from drying out on land, diverged into two primary lineages: The Synapsids and the Sauropsids. Mammals are Synapsids. Dinosaurs are Sauropsids. Mammals evolved only about 5 million years after the first dinosaurs evolved, but their lineages had been separate at that point for at least 100 million years. We now understand that mammals never evolved from reptiles. The reptile line are the Sauropsids, you see. Both reptiles (sauropsids) and synapsids (mammals are synapsids) evolved from basal amniotes. The only reason you don’t hear the word ‘synapsid’ very often is because mammals are the only synapsids left alive. The synapsids didn’t have the robust diversity that reptiles have. In the reptiles, you have Lepidosaurs (lizards, snakes, and tuataras remain), Testudines (turtles and tortoises remain), and Archosaurs (crocodilians and dinosaurs remain - yes, birds are dinosaurs). In the synapsids, it’s only Mammalia remaining, and only monotremes, marsupials and placentals. So, the reason that dinosaurs did not evolve into mammals is because mammals are from a lineage that split away from the dinosaur line a very long time before there were any dinosaurs around, and are radically different from them. On the other hand, you can take some joy in knowing that dinosaurs still exist. They didn’t all die during the asteroid strike. It turns out that birds aren’t just descended from dinosaurs - they actually are dinosaurs, after all.

Question: How do modern humans compare to Neanderthals and Denisovans in terms of appearance?
Answer: As far as I know, we only have a pure Denisovan fingerbone, so we don’t really know what they look like. Compared with Neanderthals, Sapiens are much more gracile, taller, and have smaller noses. They also have a shoulder joint that is more flexible and allows for better accurate throwing. Their skulls are more rounded, making room for larger prefrontal lobes, but a smaller average brain size. This figure standing in a German museum shows that, while Neanderthals certainly did look different, they didn’t look so different that anyone wouldn’t politely ignore it if you saw one walking down the street. Question: Is it possible for any creatures to reach the size of dinosaurs after their extinction? Is there a specific reason why no other creatures have evolved to be as large as dinosaurs?
Answer: Sure, it’s possible. The Earth’s biosphere is always changing, and we’ve destroyed entire ecosystems, devastated others, and changed the climate, triggering a mass extinction event. Huge animals need a lot of food. Unless we stop destroying literally everything, there won’t be enough food to support the evolution of a huge animal. If we actually stop destroying rainforests and let the Earth’s ecosystems recover, and leave space for wild creatures, eventually a land animal that large could evolve again. And if it does, it will probably be a dinosaur. Because dinosaurs didn’t all become extinct - we still have avian dinosaurs, which means the potential of the dinosaurian lineage is still right there in them. The reason I say that it’s more likely that a bird will evolve into an enormous animal is because Saurischian dinosaur bones are made of very dense, strong material, and they are also hollow and full of air, connected to the respiratory system. That’s what allowed the sauropod dinosaurs to reach such gargantuan sizes. The very largest sauropods show signs of stress fractures in their bones - a result of just living and moving at that tremendous size and weight. They’re at the limit of what’s possible for a land animal with a bone skeleton, and it’s all due to the clever latticework inside their hollow, lightweight bones. The bones of a Saurischian dinosaur are much stronger than a mammal bone of the same size, but weigh about the same. Birds are saurischian dinosaurs. A land mammal could never reach the size of a sauropod dinosaur, because their bones would have to be too large and heavy for it to be feasible. If they evolved denser bones, and hollow bones, they could do it - but that’s a much longer and far less likely evolutionary path than a bird simply evolving into a huge animal. It would be easier for a bird to evolve into a giant quadruped than for a mammal to evolve Saurischian dinosaur-like bones. Of course, dinosaurs ranged in size from the tiny Bee Hummingbird on up to the largest sauropods, and everything in between. Prior to the K-Pg extinction, there were plenty of small non-avian dinosaurs as well. So, ‘as large as dinosaurs’ depends on which dinosaurs you mean. There were quite a few rather large dinosaurs, but there have also been some rather large mammals. Tyrannosaurus rex on the left, Paraceratherium, an extinct relative of the rhinoceros, on the right. Mammals may not be able to become as large as a sauropod, but they can become as large as a Tyrannosaur or Triceratops. And at least one did. It became extinct 23 million years ago. And the crown of ‘largest confirmed animal to have ever lived’ still sits on the head of the Blue Whale, endangered but hanging in there, alive today. With the sea supporting its weight, it doesn’t have to worry about issues with bone strength and size.
